name: Nora Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say is confidential and your name won't be on it. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three weeks a month I lead a live-line crew in the suburbs, which means we work on lines while the power's still on, so nobody loses electricity. That's rubber gloves up to the shoulder, insulated sticks, and a lot of very slow, very careful movements from a bucket truck. The fourth week I'm at the company's training yard teaching apprentices. I love the teaching more than I expected, and what wears me out is the concentration, because live work is mentally tiring in a way people don't see.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up teaching?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My old boss, Raymond, retired and recommended me. I think it's because I'm fussy about procedure. The apprentices call me the Checklist, and I take it as a compliment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and that's about it. At work, I'd tell the apprentices to learn it anyway, because useful is still useful. Online I'd probably not bother saying anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the next ten years look like the last ten. That's fine by me. Yasmin starts university in two years, so steady is exactly what we need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. Keep the three months of savings topped up, start a small fund for Yasmin's university costs. Maybe use the chatbot a bit more for writing training notes, I've tried it a couple of times and it saved me an evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really, with a teenager about to leave home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you use the chatbot for, those couple of times?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Turning my scribbled notes on glove testing into a handout the apprentices could actually read. It got one step in the wrong order, which in live work could kill someone. So I check everything, but it was still faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the university fund work in your house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karim, my partner, is a self-employed plasterer, so his money goes up and down. We put my overtime in the fund and his good months into the mortgage. It works, mostly.

S0.say: I'd say it's a useful tool and that's about it. I'd tell the apprentices to learn it anyway because useful is still useful.
S0.think: I think the next ten years look like the last ten, which suits me. With my daughter starting university in two years, steady is what we need.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal, tops up the savings and starts a university fund for her daughter. Uses the chatbot a little more for writing training notes, checking every step.
S0.quote: It got one step in the wrong order, which in live work could kill someone.
S0.fieldNote: Nora uses AI cautiously and checks everything, which fits her live-line safety habits. Her daughter starting university in two years is a key date in her thinking. Her partner's uneven self-employed income shapes how the family budgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where training matters most. If jobs change, someone has to teach people the new way safely. I'd say that to management and I'd put my hand up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think live work holds up well, because it's slow and careful and every pole is different. The robot arms they've trialled elsewhere still need a person guiding them. I'd want to be the person teaching people how to guide them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the training manager to send me on the first course for the robotic live-line tools, once they'd been used for real somewhere. I'd use AI more for lesson plans. And I'd start turning my checklists into something the new kit could follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said once they'd been used for real somewhere. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen shiny kit arrive and get quietly put back in the shed six months later. I'm not going to teach anything I haven't seen work on a live line. That's not stubbornness, it's safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karim, more than me. There are already machines that spray plaster. If building work goes that way, the up-and-down money gets more down.

S1.say: I'd say training matters most when jobs change, because someone has to teach the new way safely. I'd put my hand up to do it.
S1.think: I think live work holds up because it's slow and careful and every pole is different. I'd want to be the one teaching people to guide the robot arms.
S1.do: Asks to go on the first robotic live-line course once the tools have proven themselves elsewhere. Uses AI more for lesson plans and turns her checklists into material the new kit can follow.
S1.quote: I'm not going to teach anything I haven't seen work on a live line.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady change as a chance to grow her teaching role. Her wait-for-proof stance comes from safety, not fear. Interestingly, she worries more about her partner's plastering than her own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow down. You can't put untested machines on live lines in two years without people getting hurt or the lights going out. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, managers, regulators, the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd have a year, maybe a year and a half, while they still need humans to supervise and certify. Then it's over, for me and for Karim at the same time. And it lands right when Yasmin's first university bills arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the holiday and any big purchases straight away and push our savings up as fast as possible. I'd ask about moving full time to the training yard, because that'd be the last job to go. And I'd sit down with Yasmin about whether to start university now or wait a year and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that conversation with Yasmin sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be angry, I think, because she's worked so hard. I'd tell her I'm not saying don't go, I'm saying let's not borrow a fortune for a degree nobody can promise will matter. That would be a horrible evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it'd hit you and Karim at the same time. What does that do to the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It wrecks it. Our whole system is one of us covers when the other's slow. If both go, the three months of savings is just three months.

S2.say: I'd say slow down, because untested machines on live lines in two years will hurt people or cause blackouts. I'd say it to managers and regulators.
S2.think: I think I'd have a year or so while humans still supervise, then it's over for both me and my partner. It lands right as my daughter's university bills arrive.
S2.do: Cancels the holiday and big purchases to build savings fast. Asks to move full time to the training yard and talks with her daughter about delaying university.
S2.feel: Scared, awake at three in the morning doing sums.
S2.quote: If both go, the three months of savings is just three months.
S2.fieldNote: The danger for her is everything hitting at once: her job, her partner's work and university costs. Her public message is about safety rather than jobs, which is typical of her. The conversation about her daughter delaying university was clearly painful to picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do it safely, so do it safely. Train people to supervise the machines and keep a human on every live job. I'd want that written into the rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me room. Yasmin would be through most of her degree, and I could become the person who certifies robot crews. I think there'd be a few years of that before even that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd get every certificate going for the new live-line equipment and offer to write the training course myself. I'd keep a bit more aside each month, maybe a hundred and fifty. And I'd tell Karim to start learning to run the plastering machines, not fight them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Karim take that advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first. He's proud of doing it by hand. But he listened when I said the same about the laser level ten years ago, and now he won't work without it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years from now you'd be forty-eight. What's the plan after the certifying work goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. I'd hope by then there's some kind of plan from the government. I'm not going to pretend I've got that bit worked out.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to do it safely, so do it safely. Keep a human on every live job and write it into the rules.
S3.think: I think five years gives me room to see my daughter through most of her degree and become someone who certifies robot crews, for a while.
S3.do: Gets every certificate for the new live-line equipment and offers to write the training course. Saves about a hundred and fifty more a month and urges her partner to learn plastering machines.
S3.feel: Anxious, but she can see a path.
S3.quote: He's proud of doing it by hand.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her build a bridge into certifying robots and gets her daughter through university first. She's honest that she has no plan after that. She nudges her partner towards the machines, using the laser level as proof he can adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get the rules, the training and the safety right. No excuses. Let's not rush the bit where people could get killed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is comfortable for me, mostly. Both kids would be through school, Yasmin done with university. I'd be fifty-three and probably teaching people to run the machines, maybe even teaching the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move gradually into training, maybe half and half in the first year. I'd learn the AI tools properly, not just now and then. And I'd tell Adam, who's twelve, to keep his options wide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a low way. It's far enough off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does keep his options wide mean to a twelve-year-old?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He wants to be a game designer, which is probably the first job the robots take. I'd tell him to learn to do things with his hands as well as screens. Just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference for you between five and ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five, I'm grabbing at the next rung. With ten, I can choose it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to get the rules, training and safety right, with no excuses. Don't rush the part where people could get killed.
S4.think: I think ten years is mostly comfortable for me, with the kids through school and university. I'd be fifty-three and teaching people to run the machines.
S4.do: Moves gradually into training, about half her time in the first year. Learns AI tools properly and encourages her son to keep his options wide.
S4.quote: With five, I'm grabbing at the next rung. With ten, I can choose it.
S4.fieldNote: The extra time lets her choose her next step instead of grabbing at it. Safety stays the core of her public message in every scenario. She steers her son towards hands-on skills as a backup.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it all lands at once: my job, Karim's work and Yasmin's university. What would help is help with university costs for kids whose parents lose their jobs, and a guarantee that people get trained to supervise the machines before the machines arrive. Not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens when it goes wrong. On a live line, a mistake isn't a typo. Somebody has to know what to do when the robot freezes halfway up with eleven thousand volts next to it.

headlineQuote: On a live line, a mistake isn't a typo.
portrait: Nora Haddad is a 43-year-old live-line crew lead who also teaches apprentices one week a month and is known for being fussy about procedure. She uses AI now and then and checks every step, because a wrong step on a live line can kill. She sees steady change as a chance to expand her teaching. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because her job, her self-employed partner's work and her daughter's university costs would all hit at once. With five or ten years she plans a move into certifying and training robot crews, and the extra time lets her choose her next step instead of grabbing at it.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her job, her partner's work and her daughter's university costs would all be hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: Help with university costs for children of people who lose their jobs, and guaranteed training to supervise the machines before they arrive.
